name: Hope (Emirates Mars Mission)
operator: MBRSC and UAE Space Agency (United Arab Emirates)
short_status: In Mars orbit since 9 February 2021 and still flying as of 23 August 2026: the UAE announced a three-year extension to 2028 on 17 February 2026, and JPL held tracking data for it through 28 May 2026.
tagline: MBRSC and UAE Space Agency (United Arab Emirates) · United Arab Emirates · Orbiter · 2021 · Multipolar Mars Operating
stats: interplanetary mission built and flown by an Arab nation
orbit period, chosen so one spacecraft sees the whole disc at every local hour
extended mission end approved in February 2026

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 19 July 2020 at 21:58:14 UT on a Mitsubishi H-IIA from Tanegashima Space Center, Japan. NASA's catalogue gives the local equivalents as 20 July, 01:58 a.m. in the UAE and 06:58 a.m. in Japan, which is why almost every account, English Wikipedia included, dates the launch 20 July. Two further sources agree on 19 July: the mission's own overview paper in Space Science Reviews gives 19 July 2020 (UTC), and JPL Horizons' EMM trajectory file, EMM_20200719-20261126_od03-195, begins at 2020-Jul-19 23:07 UT.

facts.label: Mars orbit insertion
facts.value: 9 February 2021. NASA's catalogue times the start of the 27-minute burn at about 15:41 UT Earth-received time, with completion at about 16:08 UT ERT and a one-way light time of 10 min 40 s, which puts the burn start at roughly 15:30 UT on the spacecraft's own clock. English Wikipedia prints 15:30 UTC. The two figures describe the same event measured at different ends of the link.

facts.label: Insertion cost in propellant
facts.value: About 400 kg of hydrazine, half the 800 kg the spacecraft carried at launch.

facts.label: Science orbit
facts.value: About 20,000 by 43,000 km, period about 55 hours (roughly 2.25 Martian sols), inclination 25 degrees. NASA's catalogue rounds it to roughly 22,000 by 44,000 km. Periapsis sits near the equator and its local time precesses at about the same rate Mars moves around the Sun.

facts.label: Why that orbit
facts.value: The mission's own overview paper describes it as giving global views of the lower and upper atmosphere at all local times over a nine to ten day cycle. A low, near-polar orbit of the kind most Mars orbiters use resolves fine detail but revisits each place at nearly the same hour; Hope traded resolution for coverage.

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: 1,350 kg at launch including 800 kg of hydrazine, 550 kg dry, per NASA's catalogue; the mission's overview paper gives about 1,343 kg wet and 543 kg dry. A hexagonal prism 2.37 m across and 2.90 m tall, with solar wings spanning 7.9 m.

facts.label: Power
facts.value: NASA's catalogue gives 600 W at Mars against a spacecraft requirement of 477 W. English Wikipedia's infobox instead prints 1,800 W from the two panels, which is a panel rating rather than the delivered power at Mars distance.

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: Three: the Emirates eXploration Imager (EXI), a visible and ultraviolet camera; the Emirates Mars Infrared Spectrometer (EMIRS), which maps dust, water vapour, ice and temperature in the lower and middle atmosphere; and the Emirates Mars Ultraviolet Spectrometer (EMUS), which watches hydrogen and oxygen escaping from the upper atmosphere.

facts.label: US partners
facts.value: The mission was developed with the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder, Arizona State University, and the Space Sciences Laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. English Wikipedia assigns EXI and EMUS to LASP and EMIRS to Arizona State with Northern Arizona University.

facts.label: Team
facts.value: Arabic Wikipedia gives about 200 Emirati engineers alongside about 200 scientists and engineers at the US partner institutions, with Omran Sharaf as project manager and Sarah Al Amiri as deputy project manager and science lead.

facts.label: Nominal mission
facts.value: One Martian year of science from 23 May 2021, with a two-year extension foreseen from the outset. NASA's catalogue records the plan as two years of science with the possibility of extending into 2025.

facts.label: Extension to 2028
facts.value: Announced on Tuesday 17 February 2026 by Ahmad Belhoul Al Falasi, UAE Minister of Sport and chairman of the UAE Space Agency board, at a press conference in Dubai: three further years, to 2028.

facts.label: Data releases
facts.value: The Emirates Mars Mission Science Data Center publishes on a six-month cadence. Its public news page, checked on 23 August 2026, still shows Release 16 dated 10 September 2025, covering instrument observations up to 28 February 2025, as the most recent announcement. Downloading data requires a free account, which we did not create.

facts.label: How much data
facts.value: Figures differ and so do the units. A July 2026 six-year roundup says more than 10 terabytes shared openly, in 16 released batches. AFP's report of the February 2026 announcement says the mission planned to collect one terabit and ultimately collected ten. Arabic Wikipedia gives about 12 data packages totalling 5.4 terabytes by April 2025.

facts.label: Scientific output
facts.value: More than 35 peer-reviewed papers and more than 250 conference presentations, with data used by more than 200 institutions worldwide, per the July 2026 roundup.

facts.label: Tracking
facts.value: JPL Horizons lists target -62 as Emirates Mars Mission (EMM, HOPE Probe) and returns Mars-centred state vectors for 3 September 2026 from orbit solution EMM_20200719-20261126_od03-195. Horizons states that this solution is fit to tracking data through 2026-05-28, with a predicted trajectory thereafter running to 2026-11-26. Today's vectors are therefore predicted; none of them is a measurement. What the file does establish is that JPL held real tracking data for Hope as recently as late May 2026.

timeline: The UAE commits to a Mars orbiter and gives itself six years. The mission's overview paper describes development starting in 2014 under aggressive schedule and cost constraints.
21:58:14 UT: launch on a Mitsubishi H-IIA from Tanegashima. Locally it is already 20 July in both Japan and the UAE, which is the date most accounts print.

A 27-minute burn consuming about 400 kg of hydrazine puts Hope into Mars orbit. The UAE becomes the fifth entity to place a spacecraft in orbit around Mars, after the United States, the Soviet Union, ESA and India, and the first Arab nation to do so.
Science operations formally begin, after transfer into the 20,000 by 43,000 km, 55-hour observing orbit.

The first close-up global images of Deimos are released. The UAE Space Agency puts the closest approach at about 100 km and calls it the nearest a spacecraft has come to the moon since Viking in 1977.
At a special session of a geosciences congress in Vienna, the science team presents the full Deimos dataset and argues the moon more likely formed from Mars than as a captured asteroid.
Science Data Center Release 16 makes instrument observations up to 28 February 2025 public. As of 23 August 2026 this is still the newest release announced on the centre's public news page.
Hope turns EXI and EMUS on interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar object identified in the Solar System, adding a Mars-orbit vantage point to observations made from Earth.
Five years in Mars orbit, against a nominal mission of one Martian year.
Ahmad Belhoul Al Falasi announces in Dubai that the mission is extended by three years to 2028. He tells reporters the mission had aimed to collect one terabit of atmospheric data and collected ten.
Aviation Week reports the extension, noting the agency's statement that the probe has exceeded its initial data goals by more than ten times.

A six-year roundup describes Hope as still delivering, lists more than 10 terabytes of shared data and more than 35 peer-reviewed papers, and frames the extension as preparation for the Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt, scheduled for launch in 2028.

images.caption: Hope's first science image of Mars, taken by the Emirates eXploration Imager on 10 February 2021 from about 24,700 km altitude, one day after orbit insertion, showing the north polar region and Olympus Mons catching the sunrise.
The full disc of Mars assembled from Hope EXI red, green and blue filter frames taken on 1 May 2021 during orbit 47, from a spacecraft altitude of 21,519 km, processed by Andrea Luck.

A labelled composite graphic titled 'The Ultraviolet Colors of the Red Planet', showing four false-colour ultraviolet views of Mars from the Emirates Mars Ultraviolet Spectrometer, grouped by species: hydrogen at 102.6 and 121.6 nm, oxygen at 130.4 nm and the 135.6 nm oxygen glow driven by energetic electrons, and carbon monoxide emission between 140 and 160 nm. The instrument team assembled the labelled graphic out of spectrometer data, so no single camera frame looks like this.

Omran Sharaf, project manager of the Emirates Mars Mission, speaking at the official announcement of the mission's scientific objectives at Al Bahr Palace in Dubai on 6 May 2015, in front of Arabic text reading 'First Arab probe to explore Mars'.

The sealed shipping container carrying the Hope spacecraft being lifted from a Volga-Dnepr Antonov freighter in Japan in late April 2020, after the flight from Dubai. The spacecraft itself is inside the container and not visible; the container carries the mission decal.
A full-size mockup of the Hope orbiter displayed at the International Astronautical Congress in Dubai in October 2021, showing the hexagonal bus, the two solar wings and the high-gain antenna.
